This page goes with **Chapter 2, Major Scales and Key Signatures** of Robert Hutchinson's open textbook
[*Music Theory for the 21st-Century Classroom*](https://musictheory.pugetsound.edu/mt21c/MajorScalesAndKeySignatures.html).

**You already know this.** You can sing in major tonality on movable do, find do on the staff, and read and write tonal patterns.
This chapter adds no new sounds. It gives **names** to things you already hear and write. Each section below starts from what you
know, then gives the textbook's word for it.

Press ▶ to hear an example, or **▶ Sing** to hear it sung on syllables. Click any heading to fold its section.

## What you know → what the book calls it

| You say (MLT) | The book says (Hutchinson ch. 2) |
|---|---|
| major tonality | major key, major scale |
| do, the resting tone | tonic, scale degree 1 (written 1̂) |
| do re mi fa so la ti | scale degrees 1̂ 2̂ 3̂ 4̂ 5̂ 6̂ 7̂ |
| the close steps mi–fa and ti–do | half steps |
| every other step (do–re, re–mi …) | whole steps |
| keyality (where you sing do, e.g. G) | the key's name: "G major" |
| the do signature | the key signature |

## 2.1 Half steps and whole steps

Sing the major scale up on syllables and listen to the size of each step. Two of them are smaller: **mi–fa** and **ti–do**. The book
calls a small step a **half step** (on a keyboard, the very next key) and a big one a **whole step** (two half steps).
[Read 2.1](https://musictheory.pugetsound.edu/mt21c/HalfStepsAndWholeSteps.html)

<div class="abc-ex" data-bpm="90"><script type="text/plain">
X:1
T:Do to do: the half steps are mi–fa and ti–do
M:4/4
L:1/4
K:C
C D E F | G A B c |]
w:do re mi fa so la ti do
</script></div>

So the pattern of steps in every major scale is **W W H W W W H**. That isn't a new rule to learn: it's the shape of the scale you
already sing, written down.

**On the staff.** In C, the half steps fall on E–F and B–C, where there is no black key between. That's why C major needs no sharps
or flats. Start the same pattern on another note and some letters have to change to keep the half steps on mi–fa and ti–do. That
is all a key signature is.

## 2.2 Scale degrees and their names

The book numbers the notes of the scale from do: **1̂** to **7̂**. Each also has a name.
[Read 2.2](https://musictheory.pugetsound.edu/mt21c/TheMajorScale.html)

| Syllable | Degree | Name |
|---|---|---|
| do | 1̂ | tonic |
| re | 2̂ | supertonic |
| mi | 3̂ | mediant |
| fa | 4̂ | subdominant |
| so | 5̂ | dominant |
| la | 6̂ | submediant |
| ti | 7̂ | leading tone |

*(The degree names are standard; Hutchinson's own list is in [3.3 Scale Degree Names](https://musictheory.pugetsound.edu/mt21c/ScaleDegreeNames.html).)*

You already sing **tonic** and **dominant** patterns: do–mi–so is a tonic pattern, so–ti–re a dominant pattern. Those words come
from these degree names: the patterns are built on do (the tonic) and so (the dominant).

**Do and the tonic.** Usually the same note in major, but not always the same idea. *Do* is a syllable and moves with the keyality.
*Tonic* is the resting tone of whatever key you are in. In minor you rest on **la**, and the book will call la the tonic of the minor
key (Chapter 3).

## 2.3 Key signatures are do signatures

You already find do from the key signature. Gordon calls a key signature a **do signature**: it shows where do is on the staff, and
nothing more. The same signature can be major, minor, Dorian and so on, depending on which note the music rests on (Gordon 155–156).
[Read 2.3](https://musictheory.pugetsound.edu/mt21c/MajorKeySignatures.html)

The book reads a signature as the name of a **major key**, which is the same as asking "where is do?":

- **Sharps:** the last sharp is **ti**. Do is the next note up. Last sharp F♯ → do is G → **G major**.
- **Flats:** the last flat is **fa**. Do is four notes down (or five up). With two or more flats, the second-to-last flat is do:
  B♭ E♭ → do is B♭ → **B♭ major**. One flat (B♭) → do is F.

Here is the same tune with three different do signatures. Your syllables stay the same, only the letters change:

<div class="abc-ex" data-bpm="100"><script type="text/plain">
X:1
T:Do on C: no sharps or flats
M:4/4
L:1/4
K:C
C E G E | F D B, C |]
w:do mi so mi fa re ti do
</script></div>

<div class="abc-ex" data-bpm="100"><script type="text/plain">
X:1
T:Do on G: one sharp, F♯ is ti
M:4/4
L:1/4
K:G
G B d B | c A F G |]
w:do mi so mi fa re ti do
</script></div>

<div class="abc-ex" data-bpm="100"><script type="text/plain">
X:1
T:Do on E♭: three flats, A♭ is fa
M:4/4
L:1/4
K:Eb
E G B G | A F D E |]
w:do mi so mi fa re ti do
</script></div>

**Where the book and MLT disagree.** Hutchinson reads three flats as "E♭ major or C minor". Gordon reads it as do on E♭, and the
music decides the rest: E♭ major if it rests on do, C minor if it rests on la, F Dorian if on re (Gordon 155–156). Both are
right; the book names the two keys you'll meet most often.

### Practise: name the major key

Name the major key from the signature (that is, find do). Start with up to three sharps and flats in treble clef, then open
**Settings** and add more.

<div class="drill" data-ex="keysig" data-settings="mode=major&kinds=both&most=3&clef=treble"></div>

## Bridging: from syllables to letters

The book expects you to **write** scales and key signatures from letter names. You can already write tonal patterns from a familiar
do signature (Gordon 125). To get from there to the book's tasks:

1. **Name do.** Look at the signature and say the letter of do aloud ("do is D").
2. **Sing, then spell.** Sing do re mi fa so la ti do, and say each letter as you go: D E F♯ G A B C♯ D. If a letter sounds wrong for
   the syllable, it needs an accidental.
3. **Check the half steps.** mi–fa and ti–do should be the only neighbours with no key between them.
4. **Go the other way.** Given "write A♭ major", put do on A♭, sing up, and write each letter. Then collect the accidentals: that's
   the key signature.

## Check yourself

1. In D major, which letters are mi and fa?
2. Name the major key with four sharps.
3. Name the major key with four flats.
4. Which scale degree is so? What is its name?
5. Write the steps (W or H) between each note of A major.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Answers
1. F♯ and G.
2. E major (last sharp D♯ is ti).
3. A♭ major (second-to-last flat).
4. 5̂, the dominant.
5. W W H W W W H, the same as every major scale: A B C♯ D E F♯ G♯ A.
:::

All the key-signature drills are on [Theory Drills](theory-drills.qmd?ex=keysig). Next: [Meter: Two Ways to Sort Time Signatures](meter-taxonomy.qmd)
and [Rhythm Notation from Du De](rhythm-basics.qmd). Related: [Modes: Three Meanings of One Word](modes-three-ways.qmd).
